newsitem.title: INDONESIA: RUPIAH FALLS AFTER FLOAT, BUT STABLE IN LATE TRADE.
newsitem.headline: RUPIAH FALLS AFTER FLOAT, BUT STABLE IN LATE TRADE.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah continued to stabilise against the dollar in late trading on Thursday after a steep plunge when the central bank scrapped its intervention band, dealers said.
One dealer in Singapore said the market was seeking a new equilibrium after the surprise move, seen as a managed float.
Bank Indonesia said it will no longer announce its daily intervention and conversion bands with immediate effect.
"The government has decided effective from today, August 14, the announcement of intervention and conversion bands...will be abolished," the central bank said in a statement.
Spot rupiah ranged between 2,750 and 2,790 in the afternoon, with some players seen cashing out from dollars.
The rate crashed to a low of 2,800 in thin volume before recovering to 2,760/70 at 0910 GMT from an opening of 2,648/58.

One U.S. bank dealer said players in the market were mainly from offshore but overall volume was thin. "Local operators can't do much because of the tight rupiah liquidity," the dealer said, adding overnight money was traded at around 30 percent, although that was lower than the earlier 50 percent.
One local bank dealer said operators remained cautious and wanted to know how London and New York would react to the news.
"If London and New York digest it well, I think we are likely to see the rupiah making some recovery," he said.
The dealer said swaps fell after the abolishment of the band because operators were expecting possible relief on the interest rate front.
He however said the statement from the finance minister that tight monetary and fiscal policies would be maintained pushed them up again.
Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said tight monetary and fiscal policies were in place and that their continuation would depend on developments.
One-month swap fell to 25 before rising back to 32/42. Six-month swap also increased to 135/145 from a low of 120.
"I think the band move was a good one in the medium-term. This will allow the central bank to fine-tune the market whenever it's necessary," the Singapore bank dealer said.
"Now there is no more target speculators can aim at."

"Theoretically, it's a free float," bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television in an interview. "But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course, to smooth the (adaptation) period.
"You can also call it a managed float without a band."
The bank had last fixed the intervention band at 2,378/2,682 on Wednesday.

Djiwandono noted that the Thai baht and the Philippine peso had been floated since speculative attacks on regional currencies began, while the Malaysian ringgit and the Singapore dollar were being traded without any pre-announced limits.
"We are a regional market now. We are moving together," Djiwandono said.
"In the last few weeks Indonesia is the only one which had a band, it's the only one defending the rupiah," he said adding that maintaining that position would be more and more difficult.
"We are adjusting to the new realities," he said. "The new reality in the ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) region is floating (currencies)."
Economists said the move was a positive one.
"It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," said Desmond Supple, regional currencies specialist at BZW Asia in Singapore.
"Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth."
He said it was not surprising the rupiah had plunged on the announcement but said there was scope for recovery later.

"We are going to see substantial over-shooting," Supple said. "But it (the announcement) lays the conditions for reversal of the rupiah in the long-term and bring it back to a semblance of fair value."
